1.title: Secure Access to AWS Resources
1.text: Welcome to Module one: Secure Access to A W S Resources. This module covers task statement one point one, the first task of Domain one, Design Secure Architectures, which carries thirty percent of the exam. You will learn how to protect the root user, build an authorization model with users, groups, roles and policies, give access across accounts, and govern many accounts. The exam gives you a requirement and asks you to choose the access design that fits.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Apply security best practices to the root user and to I A M, short for Identity and Access Management, users. Design an authorization model with users, groups, roles and policies. Design role-based access with A W S S T S, role switching and cross-account access. Design a security strategy for many accounts with Organizations, service control policies and Control Tower. And decide when to federate a directory service with I A M roles.

1.title: Case Check-In: Lantern and Loom Opens the Doors
1.text: At Lantern and Loom, the first access decisions have arrived. The founder still signs in as the root user. Eight engineers now share the account, and a partner photo studio must upload images. Development, test and production will soon live in separate accounts, and staff already sign in to company systems with an existing directory. Your job is to decide who gets which access, with the least privilege that works.

1.title: The Shared Responsibility Model
1.text: Every security decision starts with the shared responsibility model. A W S is responsible for the security of the cloud: the hardware, software, networking and facilities that run its services, including the physical security of the data centers. You are responsible for security in the cloud: your data, your identities and permissions, and the settings of the services you choose, such as I A M permissions, encryption choices, guest operating system patches on E C two, short for Elastic Compute Cloud,, and security groups. Your share depends on the services you choose, because managed services shift more work to A W S. Controls are inherited, shared or customer-specific. Patching is shared: A W S patches the infrastructure, and you patch your guest operating system. Exam tip: who can sign in, and what they may do, is always your side of the line.

1.title: Regions and Availability Zones
1.text: Next, the global infrastructure. A Region is a separate geographic area, and you choose the Regions where your resources run. An Availability Zone is one or more discrete data centers, with independent power, networking and connectivity, inside a Region. Zones in a Region are far enough apart to avoid shared failures, and close enough for fast synchronous replication. For access control, remember that I A M users, roles and policies are global: you define them once for the account, not once per Region. You can also enforce which Regions are allowed later, with an organization policy. Exam tip: spreading across Availability Zones protects against a data center failure, while choosing a Region is about location, latency and rules.

1.title: Protect the Root User
1.text: The root user is created with the account and has complete access, including billing. So do not use it for daily work; create an administrative user instead. Turn on multi-factor authentication for the root user; you can register up to eight devices, and a phishing-resistant type is best where possible. Never create access keys for the root user. Use a strong, unique password and a group email address, and restrict who can recover the account. Monitor root sign-ins. And when you use Organizations, you can remove root credentials from member accounts. This slide goes beyond the exam guide's wording, but root questions are common. Exam tip: the root user gets M F A, no access keys, a locked-away password, and use only for the few tasks that need it.

1.title: IAM Users, Groups and Roles
1.text: I A M has three identity building blocks. An I A M user is a person or application identity in one account, with long-term credentials such as a password and access keys. Use one only in rare cases that cannot use roles or federation. An I A M group is a collection of I A M users that lets you give the same permissions to many users; it has no credentials of its own. An I A M role is an identity that anyone authorized can assume. It has temporary credentials, issued by A W S S T S, and it suits workloads, federated staff and cross-account access. Best practice is temporary credentials for people and workloads. Exam tip: when a question offers a user with keys or a role, the role is usually the secure answer.

1.title: IAM Policy Types
1.text: You need to know five policy types. An identity-based policy is attached to a user, group or role, and it grants permissions. A resource-based policy is attached to a resource, such as a bucket or queue, and it grants permissions to named principals, even in other accounts. A permissions boundary is attached to a user or role, and it sets the maximum; it grants nothing. A service control policy is attached to an organization, an O U or an account, and it sets the maximum for member accounts; it also grants nothing. A session policy limits one role session. Exam tip: only identity-based and resource-based policies grant; the rest only limit.

1.title: Policy Evaluation: An Explicit Deny Always Wins
1.text: How does A W S decide? By default every request is denied. An explicit deny in any applicable policy always wins. Then, inside one account, identity-based and resource-based permissions combine, so one allow is enough. But when a permissions boundary or a service control policy applies, the identity policy, the boundary and the service control policy must all allow the action. For cross-account access, the caller's account and the resource's account must both allow. The figure shows the flow: an explicit deny ends in deny; otherwise the boundaries and the policies must allow; and anything else is an implicit deny. Exam tip: if one policy says Deny and another says Allow, the answer is Deny.

1.title: Least Privilege and IAM Best Practices
1.text: Least privilege means granting only the actions, resources and conditions the job needs. Start with A W S managed policies, then move to customer managed policies that fit the job. I A M Access Analyzer helps in three ways: it generates policies from CloudTrail activity, it validates the policies you write, and it finds public and cross-account access. Regularly remove unused users, roles, permissions and credentials, using last accessed information. Use conditions in policies, such as requiring M F A or T L S, short for Transport Layer Security,. And use permissions boundaries to delegate permission management safely. Exam tip: least privilege is the narrowest policy that still lets the job work.

1.title: IAM Roles and Temporary Credentials with AWS STS
1.text: A role has no password and no access keys. When you assume it, A W S S T S returns temporary credentials. Every role has two kinds of policy: a trust policy, which says who may assume it, and permissions policies, which say what it may do. The AssumeRole call is used by users or roles, in the same or another account. AssumeRoleWithSAML and AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity are used by federated users from an identity provider. E C two, Lambda and other compute services receive their role's credentials automatically. Outside A W S, I A M Roles Anywhere uses X five oh nine certificates. Exam tip: applications on A W S get a role; they never carry stored access keys.

1.title: Cross-Account Access with Roles
1.text: Here is the standard cross-account pattern. The production account creates a role, and its trust policy names the development account. The development account lets a group call S T S AssumeRole on that role. The developer then switches role in the console, or calls AssumeRole. S T S checks the trust policy and returns temporary credentials. While the developer is in the role, only the role's permissions apply; the developer's own permissions are suspended. You can require M F A on the role, and audit every use with CloudTrail. The figure shows the two accounts and the numbered steps. Exam tip: cross-account access needs two sides, a trust policy in one account and a permission to assume in the other.

1.title: Resource-Based Policy or Role?
1.text: When another account needs access, you have two main paths. With a role, the owning account creates a role, and the caller assumes it. While in the role, the caller's own permissions are suspended. It is best for many resources, or for temporary elevated access, and it works for all access. With a resource-based policy, the policy on the resource names the other account's principals. The caller keeps its own permissions, because it does not switch. It is best for one shared resource, such as a bucket, queue, topic or key, but only services that support resource policies offer it. Exam tip: one resource shared with another account means a resource-based policy; broader access means a role.

1.title: Federation with IAM Identity Center
1.text: Now federation. A W S I A M Identity Center connects workforce users to A W S accounts and to A W S managed applications. Its old name is A W S Single Sign-On, and older material may still use it. The identity source can be its own directory, Active Directory, or an external identity provider. It gives you one point of federation, with one S A M L certificate to manage. Permission sets are permissions you define once, provision into accounts, and assign to users and groups. The organization instance, in the management account, is the best practice, and it is the only type that manages access to accounts. Users sign in through the A W S access portal. Exam tip: for staff who already have identities, federate with Identity Center; for customers of your application, use Cognito, which is in the next module.

1.title: AWS Directory Service Options
1.text: A W S Directory Service offers several directories, and the exam asks you to choose. A W S Managed Microsoft A D is a real Windows Server Active Directory run by A W S. Choose it when you need actual A D features, R D S, short for Relational Database Service, for S Q L, short for structured query language, Server, or L D A P for Linux. A D Connector is a proxy to your on-premises directory, with no sync and no copy. Choose it when on-premises users must sign in to A W S with their own credentials. Simple A D is a Samba four compatible directory, with no M F A and no trust relationships. Choose it for low-scale, low-cost, basic needs. Amazon Cognito is a directory for the customers of your applications. As of the fifth of November, twenty twenty-six, the page also lists a Hybrid Edition that extends a self-managed directory, so check the editions. Exam tip: an existing on-premises directory with no copy means A D Connector, and a real Active Directory in A W S means Managed Microsoft A D.

2.title: Multiple Accounts with AWS Organizations
2.text: As you grow, use separate accounts to isolate workloads, such as development, test and production. A W S Organizations has one management account, many member accounts, and organizational units that group them. Policies attached to the root, an O U or an account flow down, so an account gets only what every parent allows. Consolidated billing gives you one bill across the organization. Run no workloads in the management account, because service control policies do not restrict it. People sign in through I A M Identity Center, and shared services are shared with R A M. Exam tip: a new requirement for isolation between environments means separate accounts under Organizations.

2.title: Service Control Policies: Guardrails, Not Grants
2.text: Service control policies are guardrails. They set the maximum permissions for I A M users and roles in member accounts, and they never grant permissions. The effective permissions are what the service control policy and the identity or resource policy both allow. They do not restrict the management account or service-linked roles, but they do restrict the root user of a member account. Keep the FullAWSAccess policy and add Deny statements, or replace it with an allow list; removing it alone blocks everything. Test on an O U first, not on the organization root. The figure shows the tree, a guardrail on the production O U, and the management account outside it. Exam tip: a service control policy caps what an account can do; it never gives anyone access.

2.title: AWS Control Tower and AWS RAM
2.text: Two services help you run many accounts. A W S Control Tower sets up and governs a multi-account environment. It orchestrates Organizations, Service Catalog and I A M Identity Center. Its key terms are the landing zone, controls that are preventive, detective or proactive, Account Factory for provisioning accounts, and a dashboard. A W S Resource Access Manager, or R A M, lets you create a resource once and share it with accounts, O U s, an organization, or, for some types, I A M roles and users. An example is a V P C, short for Virtual Private Cloud, subnet. R A M has no extra charge, and the owner keeps ownership. Exam tip: a standard multi-account setup with guardrails means Control Tower, and share instead of copy means R A M.

2.title: What the Exam Asks: Secure Access
2.text: Here is what the exam asks about secure access. Which identity: the root user, an I A M user, a group or a role. Which policy type: identity-based, resource-based, boundary, service control policy or session. Which access path: a role, a resource-based policy or R A M. Which sign-in model: I A M Identity Center, a S A M L provider, or a directory option. And which multi-account tool: Organizations, service control policies, Control Tower or R A M. Exam tip: name the identity and the account boundary first, then pick the tool.

2.title: Design Check: Lantern and Loom Opens the Doors
2.text: Here is the Design Check. Cover the right column and answer each row yourself. The founder signs in as root every day: turn on M F A for root, create no access keys, and use an administrative user for daily work. Web servers must read images from S three, short for Simple Storage Service,: an I A M role on the instances, with no stored keys. Developers must update production briefly: a cross-account role that trusts the development account, with M F A. A partner studio uploads to one bucket: a bucket policy naming the studio's account. Staff in an existing identity provider need every account: I A M Identity Center with permission sets. No account may use an unapproved Region: a service control policy on the O U. New accounts with built-in guardrails: Control Tower. Other accounts must use one V P C subnet: R A M.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. On responsibility, A W S secures the cloud, and you secure the identities, data and settings in it. For the root user, use M F A, no access keys, and roles with temporary credentials over users with keys. On policies, only identity-based and resource-based policies grant, and an explicit deny always wins. On access paths, assume a role across accounts, and use a resource policy to share one resource. And for many accounts, use Organizations, service control policies, Control Tower, R A M, I A M Identity Center, and the right directory.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Under the A W S shared responsibility model, which task is the customer's responsibility? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: choosing which I A M permissions its users get. Customers are responsible for security in the cloud, which means their data, identities and permissions. A W S is responsible for the hardware, software, networking and facilities.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Select two. Lantern and Loom's founder signs in as the root user for daily work and shares the password with the team. Which two actions fix this? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and D. Turn on M F A for the root user and store its credentials securely, and create an administrative user for daily work. Root access keys and a shared password raise exposure, and an I A M group holds I A M users, not the root user.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. A user's identity-based policy allows S three DeleteObject on a bucket. A service control policy on the user's O U explicitly denies it. What is the result? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: denied, because an explicit deny overrides any allow. Service control policies affect member accounts, not the management account, and a permissions boundary can only limit; it cannot override a deny.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Lantern and Loom's web servers on Amazon E C two must read product images from an Amazon S three bucket. Which approach is the most secure? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: attach an I A M role with S three read permissions to the instances. A role delivers temporary credentials to the instance automatically, so no long-term keys are stored. Stored keys and shared users can leak and must be rotated by hand.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Developers in Lantern and Loom's development account occasionally update objects in a production bucket. The team wants no I A M users in production and a full audit trail. What should the architect do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: create a role in production that trusts the development account, then let developers assume it. The role's trust policy names the development account, S T S issues temporary credentials, and CloudTrail records each AssumeRole call. I A M users and shared logins add long-term credentials.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. A partner photo studio, in its own A W S account, must upload photos to one S three bucket owned by Lantern and Loom. The studio's staff should keep working in their own account without switching roles. What is the simplest design? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: add a bucket policy that allows the studio's account to put objects. A resource-based policy names the other account, so its principals keep their own identities, and they also need an allow in their own account. Extra users, shared root credentials and moving the bucket do not meet the need.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. Select two. Which two statements about service control policies are correct? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and E. Service control policies set the maximum permissions available in member accounts, and they do not restrict the management account. They never grant permissions, and they do apply to the root user of a member account.

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. Lantern and Loom has several A W S accounts. Its engineers already sign in with accounts in an external S A M L identity provider. The team wants single sign-on to every account, with permissions managed in one place. Which service fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: A W S I A M Identity Center with permission sets. Cognito is for application customers, and R A M shares resources, not roles.

2.title: Practice Question 9
2.text: Question nine. A company wants employees to sign in to A W S applications and the console with their existing on-premises Active Directory credentials, without copying directory data into A W S. Which A W S Directory Service option fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: A D Connector as a proxy to the on-premises directory. It forwards sign-in requests to the on-premises domain controllers, with no synchronization. The other three hold directory data in A W S.

2.title: Practice Question 10
2.text: Question ten. Lantern and Loom is adding accounts for development, test and production. Leaders want a fast standard setup with built-in guardrails, self-service account creation and a dashboard of compliance status. Which service should the architect choose? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: A W S Control Tower. It sets up a landing zone, applies controls, offers Account Factory for self-service accounts, and shows a dashboard.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all ten answers. Question one: C. Question two: A and D. Question three: B. Question four: D. Question five: A. Question six: C. Question seven: B and E. Question eight: B. Question nine: D. Question ten: A. In Module two, we move from access to workloads and applications: networks, edge protection and application security.
